song_story.overview: Mic Drop (2017) is BTS's victory-lap answer to years of being dismissed by critics who assumed an idol group couldn't be serious musicians. It's aggressive, boastful, and specific — trophies filling up bags, sold-out world tours, chart records — aimed squarely at people who doubted them, including a direct jab at early criticism over their working-class backgrounds ('who says my spoon is dirty'). The title itself is the imagery: dropping the mic because there's nothing left to prove.
song_story.cultural_root: The song's opening line plays on 수저계급론 (spoon class theory) — a well-known Korean social metaphor sorting people into 금수저 (gold spoon, born wealthy) and 흙수저 (dirt spoon, born poor), based on the idiom 'born with a silver spoon.' BTS members have spoken openly about coming from non-wealthy families, so 금수저 여럿 패 ('I beat plenty of gold spoons') is a pointed reversal — the 흙수저 outperforming the 금수저.

verse_1.lines: Yeah, 누가 내 수저 더럽대? / I don't care, 마이크 잡음 금수저 여럿 패 / 버럭해 잘 못 익은 것들 스테끼 여러 개 / 거듭해서 씹어줄게 스타의 저녁에 / World business (Bang, bang) 핵심 / 섭외 1순위 (Clap, clap) 매진 / 많지 않지 이 class 가칠 만끽 / 좋은 향기에 악췬 반칙 / Mic, mic bungee, bright light, 전진 / 망할 거 같았겠지만 I'm fine, sorry / 미안해, Billboard, 미안해, worldwide / 아들이 넘 잘나가서 미안해, 엄마 / 대신해줘 니가 못한 효도 / 우리 콘서트 절대 없어 포도
verse_1.literal: Who says my spoon is dirty? / I don't care — once I grab the mic I beat plenty of gold spoons / I get furious at half-baked ones, several steaks / I'll keep chewing them up at the star's dinner / world business — the core / first choice for booking — sold out / not many can taste this kind of class / good fragrance next to a bad smell is a foul
verse_1.context: 수저 (spoon) here is entirely metaphor — 금수저 (gold spoon) means born rich, and the verse turns a rap battle into a direct response to critics who assumed idols couldn't have real skill or hardship behind them.

chorus.lines: I do it, I do it, 넌 맛없는 라따뚜이 / 혹 배가 아프다면 고소해, sue it / 트로피들로 백이 가득해 (가득해, 가득해) / Hater들은 벌써 학을 떼 (학을 떼) / 이미 황금빛, 황금빛 나의 성공 / I'm so firin', firin', 성화봉송 / 너는 황급히, 황급히 도망 숑숑 / 내 손에 트로피, 아, 너무 많아 / 너무 heavy 내 두 손이 모잘라 (Turn it up now) / 발, 발 조심, 너네 말, 말 조심 / Lodi-dodi, 아, 너무 바빠 / 너무 busy 내 온몸이 모잘라 (Turn it up now) / (발, 발 조심, 너네 말, 말 조심) / 이거 완전 네 글자, 사필귀정, ah
chorus.literal: Did you see my bag? Trophies fill the whole bag / how do you think about that? Haters already gave up / already golden, golden, my success / I'm so firing, firing, like an Olympic torch relay / you're hastily, hastily running away / how dare you, how dare you, how dare you
chorus.context: 학을 떼다 (hageul tteda) is an idiom meaning to be utterly exhausted/fed up with something, here used for haters finally giving up. 성화봉송 (torch relay) compares his momentum to the Olympic flame being carried forward — unstoppable, ceremonial, impossible to put out.

hook.lines: Once upon a time, 이솝우화 fly / 네 현실을 봐라 쌔 쌤통 / 지금 죽어도 난 개행복 (Turn it up) / 이번엔 어느 나라 가? (Ooh) / 비행기 몇 시간을 타? (Hey) / 무대에서 탈진, MIC drop, bam / 트로피들로 백이 가득해 (가득해, 가득해) / Hater들은 벌써 학을 떼 (학을 떼) / 이미 황금빛, 황금빛 나의 성공 / I'm so firin', firin', 성화봉송 / 너는 황급히, 황급히 도망 숑숑 / 내 손에 트로피, 아, 너무 많아 / 너무 heavy 내 두 손이 모잘라 (Turn it up now) / 발, 발 조심, 너네 말, 말 조심
hook.literal: So many trophies in my hands, ah / too heavy, my two hands aren't enough — turn it up now / mic drop, mic drop / watch your step, watch your words / lodi-dodi, ah, so busy / too busy, my whole body isn't enough — turn it up now / mic drop, mic drop
hook.context: 발 조심, 말 조심 — 'watch your step, watch your words' — is a double warning: literal (don't trip over how successful I am) and figurative (be careful what you say about me), delivered as a near-threat wrapped in playful rhythm.

bridge.lines: Lodi-dodi, 아, 너무 바빠 / 너무 busy 내 온몸이 모잘라 (Turn it up now) / (발, 발 조심, 너네 말, 말 조심) / 더 볼 일 없어 / 마지막 인사야 / 할 말도 없어 / 사과도 하지 마 / 더 볼 일 없어 / 마지막 인사야 / 할 말도 없어 / 사과도 하지 마 / 잘 봐, 넌 그 꼴 나지 / 우린 탁 쏴 마치 콜라지 / 너의 각막 깜짝 놀라지 / 꽤, 꽤 폼나지, 포-포-폼나지, yeah
bridge.literal: This is exactly four characters: 사필귀정 (things return to their rightful place) / once upon a time, Aesop's fable, fly / look at your reality, ah, serves you right / even if I die right now, I'm ridiculously happy / which country am I going to this time? / how many hours will the flight be? / yeah, I'm on the mountain, yeah, I'm on the bay / exhausted on stage, mic drop, bam
bridge.context: 사필귀정 (sapilgwijeong) is a four-character Sino-Korean idiom (사자성어) meaning 'everything eventually returns to what is right/just' — used here to frame BTS's success as deserved justice rather than luck, directly answering critics.

artist_context: Mic Drop later got a high-profile Steve Aoki remix featuring Desiigner, which is a different, longer track from the original album version — worth noting since the two versions are easy to mix up when sourcing audio.
honorific_level: informal/aggressive — 반말 throughout, delivered as direct confrontation toward unnamed critics ('haters')

grammar_highlights.usage: 사필귀정 (things return to what's right) is a classical Chinese-origin idiom still used in everyday Korean for a sense of cosmic justice — using one signals both wit and education.
Idiom meaning to be worn out/fed up with something to the point of giving up on it. Here, haters are the ones who 학을 떼 — finally exhausted and quitting.
가칠 만끽 — 'fully savoring the value/worth [of this].' 만끽하다 means to enjoy something to the fullest, often used for savoring a hard-earned moment.
